title: "Your Groceries, Measured in Minutes of Work"
subtitle: "Sticker shock is real. But paychecks grew too, and only a few items actually got harder to afford."
author: "SixtyEight95"
date: "2026-11-11"

---

```{r setup}
source("../../R/fred.R")
source("../../R/groceries_data.R")
library(plotly)
library(knitr)

pct <- function(x) paste0(ifelse(x > 0, "+", ""), round(x * 100), "%")
plain_pct <- function(x) paste0(round(x * 100), "%")

item_row <- function(name) grocery_summary %>% filter(item == name)
coffee <- item_row("Coffee (lb)")
beef   <- item_row("Ground beef (lb)")
eggs   <- item_row("Eggs (dozen)")
milk   <- item_row("Milk (gallon)")

since_1985   <- grocery_summary %>% filter(!is.na(minutes_1985))
cheaper_1985 <- sum(since_1985$minutes_change_1985 < 0)

wage_growth <- wage_now / wage_2019 - 1
months_label <- paste(format(last_12, "%B %Y"), "to", format(latest_month, "%B %Y"))
```

Everyone has a grocery receipt that made them wince. Eggs, beef, coffee: prices really did jump after
2019. But there's a piece missing from most of those conversations: **paychecks went up too.**

So instead of asking "how much does it cost?", we asked a different question: **how long do you have to
work to buy it?**

## The short answer

::: {.callout-note appearance="simple"}
Since 2019, average hourly pay is up **`r plain_pct(wage_growth)`**. That kept most groceries about as affordable as
they were. The real exceptions are **coffee (`r pct(coffee$minutes_change_2019)`)**, **ground beef
(`r pct(beef$minutes_change_2019)`)**, and **eggs (`r pct(eggs$minutes_change_2019)`)**, which genuinely take more of
your work time than they did in 2019.
:::

## What "minutes of work" means

We take the average price of an item and divide it by what the average worker earns per hour, before
taxes. The answer is how many minutes of work it takes to pay for it.

For example, a gallon of milk costs about **`r dollars(milk$price_now)`** today. The average worker earns about
**`r dollars(wage_now)` an hour**, so that gallon takes about **`r round(milk$minutes_now, 1)` minutes** of work. In 2019 milk
was cheaper, **`r dollars(milk$price_2019)`**, but pay was lower too (`r dollars(wage_2019)` an hour), so it took about
**`r round(milk$minutes_2019, 1)` minutes**. Same as now.

This works across any time period without needing to adjust for inflation, because prices and paychecks
are measured in the same year's dollars.

## 2019 vs. today

```{r since 2019}
#| fig-height: 5.5
since_2019 <- grocery_summary %>%
  mutate(item = fct_reorder(item, minutes_change_2019),
         direction = case_when(minutes_change_2019 >  0.05 ~ "Takes more work",
                               minutes_change_2019 < -0.05 ~ "Takes less work",
                               TRUE                        ~ "About the same"))

p <- ggplot(since_2019, aes(y = item)) +
  geom_segment(aes(x = minutes_2019, xend = minutes_now, yend = item, color = direction,
                   text = paste0(item,
                                 "<br>2019: ", round(minutes_2019, 1), " min (", dollars(price_2019), ")",
                                 "<br>Today: ", round(minutes_now, 1), " min (", dollars(price_now), ")",
                                 "<br>Change in work time: ", pct(minutes_change_2019))),
               linewidth = 1.2) +
  geom_point(aes(x = minutes_2019), color = "grey50", size = 2) +
  geom_point(aes(x = minutes_now, color = direction), size = 3) +
  scale_color_manual(values = c("Takes more work" = "#C53030", "About the same" = "grey55",
                                "Takes less work" = "#2A9D8F")) +
  theme_minimal() +
  labs(x = "Minutes of work", y = NULL, color = NULL)

ggplotly(p, tooltip = "text") %>%
  layout(legend = list(orientation = "h", y = 1.08)) %>%
  config(displayModeBar = FALSE)
```

Grey dot = 2019. Colored dot = today (average of `r months_label`). Hover for prices.

Prices on every item went up, by `r plain_pct(min(grocery_summary$price_change_2019))` to
`r plain_pct(max(grocery_summary$price_change_2019))`. But for most of the list, pay kept pace or did better.

## Why coffee, beef, and eggs broke away

These three each had their own supply problem, unrelated to the general price increases since 2020:

- **Coffee:** Bad harvests in Brazil and Vietnam, the two biggest growers, sent world coffee prices to
  record highs in 2024 and 2025.
- **Beef:** Years of drought shrank the U.S. cattle herd to its smallest size in decades. Fewer cattle
  means pricier beef, and herds take years to rebuild.
- **Eggs:** Bird flu outbreaks forced farms to cull millions of hens. Eggs hit their most expensive point
  in this data in **`r format(eggs$peak_date, "%B %Y")`**, at **`r round(eggs$peak_minutes, 1)` minutes** of work for a dozen.

## The long view: most groceries are cheaper than in 1985

Here's the part that surprises people. Of the `r nrow(since_1985)` items we can track back to 1985,
**`r cheaper_1985` take less work to buy today than they did then.**

```{r long view}
#| fig-height: 6
long_items <- c("Ground beef (lb)", "Coffee (lb)", "Eggs (dozen)", "Bacon (lb)",
                "Cheddar cheese (lb)", "White bread (lb)")

long_view <- grocery_monthly %>%
  filter(item %in% long_items, year(date) >= 1985) %>%
  mutate(item = factor(item, levels = long_items))

p2 <- ggplot(long_view, aes(date, minutes, group = item,
                            text = paste0(item, "<br>", format(date, "%b %Y"), ": ",
                                          round(minutes, 1), " min (", dollars(price), ")"))) +
  geom_line(color = "#1F4E5A", linewidth = 0.5) +
  facet_wrap(~item, ncol = 2, scales = "free_y") +
  expand_limits(y = 0) +
  theme_minimal() +
  labs(x = NULL, y = "Minutes of work")

ggplotly(p2, tooltip = "text") %>% config(displayModeBar = FALSE)
```

The exception is **ground beef**: `r round(beef$minutes_1985, 1)` minutes of work per pound in 1985,
`r round(beef$minutes_now, 1)` minutes today, near its highest level since the government started tracking it in 1984.

Farming, shipping, and stores all got more efficient over 40 years, and for most foods that kept
prices rising slower than pay.

## Every item we tracked

```{r table}
grocery_summary %>%
  arrange(desc(minutes_change_2019)) %>%
  transmute(Item = item,
            `Price 2019` = dollars(price_2019),
            `Price today` = dollars(price_now),
            `Minutes 2019` = round(minutes_2019, 1),
            `Minutes today` = round(minutes_now, 1),
            `Change in work time` = pct(minutes_change_2019),
            `Since 1985` = ifelse(is.na(minutes_change_1985), "–", pct(minutes_change_1985))) %>%
  kable(align = "lrrrrrr",
        caption = paste0("Today = average of ", months_label,
                         ". Milk and potatoes data start after 1985."))
```

## The fine print

- **This is the average worker, before taxes.** Your own minutes depend on your pay. If you earn less
  than average, every item takes longer.
- **These are national average prices.** Your store, your city, and brand choices will differ.
- **Groceries aren't the whole budget.** Housing, childcare, and health care have their own stories.
  We'll get to those.

## The bottom line

Grocery prices feel brutal because the dollar amounts jumped fast. Measured in time, most of the cart costs
about what it did before the pandemic, and less than it did 40 years ago. The items that truly got harder
to afford are coffee, beef, and eggs, each for its own reason.

---

**How we did this.** Prices are U.S. city-average retail prices from the
[Bureau of Labor Statistics](https://www.bls.gov/cpi/factsheets/average-prices.htm), and pay is average
hourly earnings of production and nonsupervisory employees (about 80% of private-sector workers), also
from the BLS. Both were pulled from [FRED](https://fred.stlouisfed.org/). Minutes of work = price ÷ hourly
pay × 60, calculated month by month. "Today" is the average of the last 12 months of data.
